name: Stedi
tagline: API-first healthcare clearinghouse: eligibility checks, claims, and X12 EDI translated into JSON.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: Stedi is two things bolted together: a nice JSON API over X12 EDI, and a clearinghouse that is actually connected to hundreds of insurance payers. The first half is a parser, and a coding agent can absolutely write you an X12 270/271/837/835 parser and builder in an afternoon. The second half is trading partner connections, payer enrollments, SFTP and AS2 plumbing, HIPAA obligations, and a business entity that payers will actually transact with, none of which you can generate. If you are a provider or a health tech company, the thing you are buying is reach into the payer network, not the SDK. Build the parser if you want to understand your own data; do not expect to route a real eligibility check through it.
coreLoopDIY: A local X12 toolkit that parses 270/271/837/835 files into clean JSON, validates segment structure, and renders a readable eligibility or remittance view in a browser.
requirements: Sample X12 files you are legally allowed to hold
A copy of the relevant X12 implementation guide to check segment semantics
Real payer connectivity, which you will not have
whatYouLose: Connections to the payer network, which is the entire product
Payer enrollment handling and trading partner onboarding
Real-time eligibility responses instead of files you already had
HIPAA-aligned hosting, audit trails, and a BAA someone will sign
Per-payer quirk handling, where two payers technically follow the same spec and still disagree
moatNotes: The hard part is not the format, it is being a party that hundreds of payers already exchange transactions with.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because healthcare data exchange is a permissioned network, not a file format. Anyone can learn X12 in a week of misery, but nobody can self-serve their way into being a recognized clearinghouse with live payer links, enrollment workflows, and a BAA. Teams pay Stedi to skip a year of integration work and inherit connectivity that would otherwise require contracts, testing cycles, and patience with payer IT departments. The clean API is the pleasant part; the boring institutional plumbing is the part worth money.
notes: The parser is a weekend, the clearinghouse is not. The moat is live connectivity to hundreds of payers plus the compliance posture that lets you touch the data at all.
prompt:
Build a local X12 EDI inspector for healthcare transactions. This is a parsing and viewing tool, not a clearinghouse: it never sends anything to a payer.

Stack, no substitutions:
- TypeScript, Node 20, Fastify for the tiny local server
- No database, files live on disk in ./data
- Plain HTML plus a single vanilla JS file for the UI, no framework
- Vitest for tests

What to build:
1. A parser module that reads raw X12 (ISA/GS/ST envelopes) and produces a structured tree: interchange, functional groups, transaction sets, segments, elements, composites. Respect the delimiters declared in the ISA segment instead of hardcoding * and ~.
2. Transaction-specific mappers for these set types, each returning clean JSON: 270 and 271 (eligibility request and response), 837 (claim), 835 (remittance advice). Map only the common segments: subscriber, payer, provider, service dates, EB benefit lines for 271, CLP and SVC lines for 835. Mark unmapped segments as passthrough rather than dropping them.
3. A structural validator that reports unbalanced envelopes, bad segment counts in SE/GE/IEA, unknown segment IDs, and elements that violate declared min/max length. Output a list of findings with segment index and a plain-English message.
4. A CLI: `npm run parse -- ./data/sample.271 --json` prints mapped JSON, `--tree` prints the raw segment tree, `--validate` prints findings.
5. A local web UI on http://localhost:3000 that lists files in ./data, shows a chosen file three ways: raw segments with hover tooltips naming each element, mapped JSON, and validation findings. Include a readable eligibility summary view for 271 files: active or inactive coverage, plan name, copay and deductible amounts from EB lines.
6. An 835 remittance view: claim-level paid versus billed, adjustment reason codes with descriptions from a small local lookup table you ship as JSON.

Explicitly out of scope: any network transmission, SFTP, AS2, payer enrollment, authentication, accounts, telemetry, cloud anything.

Include three small synthetic sample files in ./data (one 271, one 837, one 835) that you author yourself, clearly marked synthetic. Include tests for delimiter handling, envelope balance checks, and one 271 mapping. Write a README that states plainly: this tool reads EDI you already have, it cannot check eligibility with a real payer, and real-world use requires a HIPAA review you have not done.
